# Cloud-Based Train Control in Urban Rail: Recent Developments, Architecture, and the Safety Boundary

Cloud-based train control is advancing, but the evidence through 13 September 2026 describes a layered transition rather than a wholesale replacement of conventional CBTC. Urban railways now have operational cloud platforms for information systems, cloud-based ATS and integrated supervision, private-5G train communications, edge-computing pilots, and field-tested virtualized signaling components. The strongest direct demonstrations of cloud-hosted or cloud-ready vital functions are Siemens’ SIL4 DS3 interlocking at Achau, Austria, live CBTC and interlocking demonstrations at the Singapore Rail Test Center in November 2025, and Siemens’ cloud-native Signaling X interlocking trial under live tram passengers in Rostock, Germany, announced on 10 September 2026. However, no supplied evidence establishes a routine, full-line revenue deployment in which all vital urban-CBTC functions—ATP, ATO, VOBC, zone control, computer interlocking, and movement-authority logic—are hosted in a cloud environment.

Most current metro examples concern a different layer: cloud information platforms, ATS, monitoring, maintenance, data integration, or the communications bearer that carries CBTC traffic. The key technologies are private cloud and edge computing, virtualization and containers, commercial off-the-shelf servers, private 5G or FRMCS, network slicing, deterministic networking and time synchronization, redundant safety architectures, IoT data platforms, digital twins, and carefully bounded uses of artificial intelligence. Their practical value is potentially large—faster hardware refresh, shared computing, easier expansion, and better monitoring—but their safety case remains more demanding than an ordinary cloud migration because communications, compute infrastructure, software changes, cyberattacks, and failover behavior all become part of the railway assurance argument.

This report first defines the different meanings of “cloud-based train control.” It then catalogs recent deployments, trials, products, and research; explains a representative cloud-edge architecture; examines the enabling technologies; covers safety, reliability, cybersecurity, standards, and certification; compares cloud-edge designs with conventional on-premises CBTC; and closes by separating commercially demonstrated capabilities from research-stage proposals and identifying the most credible near-term directions.

## 1. What “cloud-based train control” means

### CBTC is more than a cloud application

Communications-based train control, or CBTC, is a continuous train-control system built around three capabilities: high-resolution train-location determination independent of track circuits, continuous high-capacity bidirectional train-to-wayside communications, and train-borne and wayside processors capable of performing vital automatic train-protection functions. Automatic train operation and automatic train supervision are associated functions that can be added to the protection layer. This functional definition is reflected in IEEE Std 1474.1 and summarized in [Cisco’s CBTC guidance](https://blogs.cisco.com/industrial-iot/benefits-and-challenges-in-deploying-communications-based-train-control-cbtc).

In a conventional urban CBTC system, the principal elements are usually:

- The vehicle onboard controller, or VOBC, which receives train speed and location information, calculates or enforces protection functions, and interfaces with traction, braking, doors, and the driver or automatic-operation equipment.
- The zone controller, or ZC, which maintains the state of the controlled railway area and calculates movement authorities using train and infrastructure information.
- The computer interlocking, or CI, which prevents conflicting routes and controls points, signals, platform doors, and related wayside equipment.
- Automatic train supervision, or ATS, which manages schedules, displays train positions, supports dispatching, and coordinates operational responses.
- The data communication system, or DCS, which provides the wired and wireless communication paths connecting the train, wayside, stations, and operations control center.
- Sensors and input-output units, including odometry, balises or transponders, axle counters, point machines, signals, platform doors, and train interfaces.

The DCS does not itself make the safety decision, but it transports a large amount of safety-related information. A 2021 study of the CBTC data-communication subsystem describes DCS as accounting for approximately 55% of the system in its design and application-engineering context and warns that a DCS failure can cause driving failure or major operational and safety consequences. The study also emphasizes synchronized clocks, redundant wired and wireless networks, self-healing rings, and hot backup for continuous operation. These are design requirements and analyses, not a universal measured availability statistic. ([CBTC data-communication study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13198-021-01055-5))

CBTC can use fixed-block or moving-block principles. Moving block calculates a continuously updated safe separation envelope rather than relying only on fixed track sections. That can support shorter headways, but the resulting capacity depends on braking performance, dwell time, station design, timetable discipline, platform doors, route conflicts, and operating rules as well as signaling computation. Moving a computation from a cabinet to a cloud does not automatically create more capacity.

### Cloud-based control is an architectural family

“Cloud-based train control” is used for several materially different systems. The distinction matters because evidence from a cloud video platform cannot be transferred to a cloud-hosted movement-authority controller.

| Architecture category | Functions commonly hosted or supported | Typical evidence through September 2026 | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|---|
| Urban-rail information cloud | Data centers, information sharing, passenger services, maintenance, video, GIS, desktops, reporting | Shenzhen and Wuhan urban-rail cloud programs; Huawei multi-line cloud platforms | That vital train-control logic runs in the cloud |
| Cloud ATS or integrated supervision | ATS services, timetable data, alarms, station monitoring, electromechanical supervision | Cloud ATS and ISCS research, production/disaster-recovery data centers, station backup modes | That ATP, ZC, CI, or VOBC logic is cloud-hosted |
| Private 5G or cloud-edge communications | Train-to-ground bearer, backhaul, telemetry, CCTV, TCMS, ATS data, network slicing | Wuhan, Mumbai Metro Line 3, CAF/Cellnex, Hitachi, 5GRAIL and FRMCS trials | A safety case for cloud-based movement authority |
| Virtualized vital signaling | Interlocking, RBC, or proposed VOBC/ZC/CI functions on COTS servers or virtual machines | Siemens DS3 and Signaling X demonstrations and trials; Achau live mainline interlocking | A routine full-line urban cloud-CBTC deployment |
| Cloud-edge research control | Cloud-hosted logic, edge MPC, AI control, digital twins, autonomous CBTC models | SDTC, ECCBTC, cloud-edge autonomous-control papers and simulations | Field performance, certification, or commercial acceptance |

A private railway cloud is also not synonymous with a public hyperscale cloud. In the deployments and proposals described by the supplied sources, the more credible safety-oriented model is an operator-controlled private cloud or a geographically separated pair of private data centers, connected by managed fiber and bounded railway networks. Public 5G or carrier infrastructure may be used for non-vital services, backhaul, or carefully isolated slices, but the evidence does not show internet-routed public-cloud movement-authority logic in routine metro operation.

### The evidence boundary

The most important finding is therefore negative only in a carefully defined sense: the supplied evidence does not show a complete, independently assessed, network-wide urban cloud-CBTC deployment with all vital functions hosted in the cloud. That does not mean cloud technology is absent from urban rail. It means the field has progressed through adjacent layers and partial vital functions.

China’s T/CAMET 11004-2020, effective from 1 March 2021, is an important example of institutionalization. It specifies a cloud-platform network architecture for urban-rail information systems, covering transmission, local-area, train-ground wireless, and onboard networks across metro, light rail, trams, monorail, maglev, and other modes. Its scope is network architecture for cloud-based information systems; the standard entry does not provide a named safety-certified cloud-CBTC deployment. ([T/CAMET 11004-2020](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/ae7fc2670f4b47d7eb44e0cdfcdf8ba0))

A separate T/CAMET CBTC standard, published in December 2024 and effective from April 2025, covers operating, system, performance, functional, interface, electromagnetic-compatibility, and environmental requirements for CBTC design, research, certification, and acceptance. It applies across several urban-rail modes, but the supplied standard record does not identify a cloud-specific certification result. ([T/CAMET 04037-2024](https://ndls.cnis.ac.cn/standard/detail/4b561429cd1244f715bff44e9629861f))

The terminology is not merely academic. A source may say that CBTC traffic is carried on a 5G network, that a line uses an urban-rail cloud, or that an ATS system is virtualized. Each statement can be true without showing that the cloud has assumed the safety-critical responsibility for detecting a train, calculating a movement authority, preventing a conflicting route, or commanding an emergency brake.

## 2. Recent developments and named examples

### Vital or signaling-focused developments

The clearest developments are best understood as a progression from safety-certified COTS computing, to test-center demonstrations, to a live urban operational trial.

| Project or system | Operator, vendor, and location | Date and maturity | Urban-rail application or scope | Evidence boundary |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DS3 digital interlocking at Achau | ÖBB-Infrastruktur AG and Siemens Mobility; Achau station on the Pottendorfer Line south of Vienna, Austria | Field trials began in December 2018; live operation began 18 November 2020 | SIL4 digital interlocking on commercial off-the-shelf servers | Mainline station reference, not an urban metro cloud-CBTC deployment |
| Signaling X at Singapore Rail Test Center | Siemens Mobility; Singapore | Live demonstration on 12 November 2025 | CBTC and interlocking functions on COTS hardware through DS3 | Test-center demonstration, not stated revenue service |
| Signaling X at Rostock Hauptbahnhof | Siemens Mobility and Rostocker Straßenbahn AG; Germany | Trial operation announced 10 September 2026 | Software-defined interlocking beneath a live tram tunnel serving lines 2, 3, 5, and 6 | Live urban trial with paying passengers; outcome, duration, equipment coverage, and acceptance details unavailable |
| TSTCBTC 2.0 | TST, Shanghai Metro; Shanghai Metro Line 5, China | SIL4 platform certificate in 2015; implementation from 2016; revenue service on the south extension in December 2018 | Dual-redundancy, moving-block CBTC and interlocking/ATP integration | Operational high-availability CBTC, but not cloud-hosted |
| BART CBTC modernization | Bay Area Rapid Transit and Hitachi Rail STS; San Francisco Bay Area, United States | Contract awarded in 2020; approximately eleven-year phased program | Test-track proof followed by deployment in eight geographic phases | Conventional CBTC modernization; the agency does not identify it as cloud-based |

#### Siemens DS3 and the significance of Achau

Siemens introduced the Distributed Smart Safe System, or DS3, in 2020 as a redundant safety platform for railway applications running on standard COTS servers. The platform separates signaling software from specialized hardware and is intended to support digital interlockings and other safety-related applications. Siemens’ account of the Achau project describes joint field trials beginning in December 2018 and live operation on 18 November 2020. It calls the project the first approval of a SIL4 interlocking based on COTS hardware. ([Siemens DS3 account](https://assets.new.siemens.com/siemens/assets/api/uuid:d71c5c42-dbd6-4b7f-8b42-9876a30f4cac/HQMOPR202011176063EN.pdf))

The architectural importance is hardware independence. In a conventional signaling installation, the certified safety function may be tightly coupled to a particular hardware platform. DS3 instead attempts to make the certified execution environment and safety mechanisms the stable object while permitting the underlying server hardware to be refreshed. The supplied Siemens material describes virtualized signaling components, redundant computing, and support for centralized and geographically redundant configurations.

This is strong evidence for safety-critical virtualization and COTS computing, but the application boundary matters. Achau is a mainline station on an Austrian railway, not a full urban metro route with cloud-hosted VOBC, moving-block ZC, and metro-wide operational integration. It demonstrates that a certified safety platform can operate on general-purpose hardware; it does not by itself demonstrate a complete cloud-CBTC architecture.

#### Singapore: a live test-center demonstration

Siemens describes Signaling X as a cloud-ready signaling platform for urban mobility and reports live CBTC operation at the Singapore Rail Test Center on 12 November 2025. The demonstration used safety-critical CBTC and interlocking functions on COTS hardware through DS3. The supplier’s urban-mobility page explicitly characterizes Singapore as a test-center demonstration rather than a citywide revenue deployment. ([Siemens Signaling X urban mobility reference](https://www.mobility.siemens.com/global/en/portfolio/references/signaling-x-for-urban-mobility.html); [status comparison of Singapore and Rostock](https://www.europesays.com/germany/89984/))

Singapore is significant because it moves beyond a mainline interlocking reference into an urban-CBTC test environment. It still remains a controlled test-center result. The supplied account does not disclose the exact equipment coverage, duration, independent acceptance authority, or whether the demonstration represented a complete operational metro line.

#### Rostock: the first stated live urban trial

On 10 September 2026, Siemens Mobility and Rostocker Straßenbahn AG announced trial operation of Signaling X in the tram tunnel beneath Rostock Central Station. The software-defined interlocking is based on DS3 and standard IT equipment. The section serves tram lines 2, 3, 5, and 6 and carries paying passengers. Siemens and associated reporting describe this as the first stated implementation of the Signaling X architecture in a real-world German urban public-transport environment. ([RailwayPro report](https://www.railwaypro.com/wp/siemens-is-testing-signaling-x-in-germany-for-urban-rail-transport/); [Rostock trial report](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/327377/20260911/siemens-runs-cloud-rail-signaling-under-live-german-tram-passengers-innotrans-debut-11-days-out.htm))

Rostock is more operationally consequential than a test-center demonstration because it places the system beneath live service. It also tests the urban conditions that are absent from a simple station interlocking reference: frequent stop-start cycles, mixed tram movements, tunnel operations, short routes, and passenger-service consequences.

The available evidence is still preliminary. The announcement does not report the trial duration, measured latency, failure and recovery statistics, acceptance authority, number of controlled points or routes, or the status of other CBTC functions such as ATP, ATO, ZC, or VOBC. It establishes a live urban interlocking trial, not a complete full-line cloud-CBTC deployment. No post-trial performance or commercial-readiness result was available in the supplied material by the cutoff date.

Siemens describes an operator-controlled private Signaling Data Center rather than a shared public cloud. The reported architecture uses physically separate data centers and claims that a secondary center can assume control within milliseconds of a primary failure. Those are architecture claims and reported validation statements; the Rostock outcome itself remains unavailable. The same supplier material claims up to 20% higher operational efficiency and up to 30% energy savings in specified Signaling X and ATO contexts, but the supplied source gives no baseline, calculation method, measurement period, or independent audit. ([Rostock evidence and claim qualifications](https://www.europesays.com/germany/89984/))

#### Operational CBTC comparators that are not cloud-based

The distinction between cloud signaling and advanced conventional CBTC is visible in TSTCBTC 2.0. TST reports that its system received a platform-level SIL4 certificate in February 2015, underwent field testing in October 2015, was implemented on Shanghai Metro Line 5 from September 2016, and completed a seamless cutover on the existing section in October 2018. The south extension entered revenue service at the end of December 2018. TST describes dual CBTC redundancy, moving block, bidirectional ATP/ATO, and interlocking-ATP integration. ([TSTCBTC 2.0 project history](https://www.thalessec.com.cn/2020/03/08/high-availability-tstcbtc-2-0-independently-developed-by-tst/))

This example is relevant because it shows that high availability, moving block, driverless operation, and successful brownfield cutover are not uniquely cloud capabilities. TST’s claims are vendor-reported and do not supply a cloud comparison, but they provide a useful baseline: an operator can obtain sophisticated and highly redundant CBTC without relocating vital logic to a cloud.

BART supplies another migration comparator. BART awarded Hitachi Rail STS a design-build contract in September 2020 and issued notice to proceed in November 2020. The agency describes an approximately eleven-year program beginning with test-track validation and continuing through eight geographic phases. It projects an increase in Transbay core capacity from 24 to 30 trains per hour per direction, with interim targets of 28 trains per hour in 2030 and up to 30 in 2032. The program includes replacement of approximately 50-year-old cables and extensive design, field survey, installation, and construction oversight. BART does not identify this CBTC system as cloud-based. ([BART train-control modernization](https://www.bart.gov/about/projects/traincontrol))

The lesson is not that cloud migration must take eleven years. It is that train-control migration is a system program involving wayside equipment, vehicles, cables, testing, cutover, operations, and safety acceptance. Cloud computing changes the location and lifecycle of some functions; it does not remove the surrounding railway assets.

### Urban cloud platforms, ATS, and private wireless

Much more urban-rail cloud activity is already operational when the word “cloud” refers to information systems, supervision, data management, or communications.

#### Shenzhen Metro Lines 6 and 10

Shenzhen Metro Lines 6 and 10 opened on 18 August 2020 as the first Chinese metro lines reported to comprehensively apply Huawei’s Urban Rail Cloud Solution. The case describes cloud computing, AI, big data, and 5G supporting a unified digital platform for metro production, management, and services. Line 6 is reported as 49.4 km with 27 stations, while Line 10 is reported as 29.31 km with 24 stations. Huawei’s account does not identify a cloud-hosted ATP, ATO, ZC, CI, or VOBC. Its AirFlash solution uploads onboard CCTV and monitoring data to the Urban Rail Cloud for equipment management and status analysis. ([Huawei Shenzhen Urban Rail Cloud account](https://investadvocateng.com/2020/10/26/transforming-how-we-move-huaweis-urban-rail-cloud-solution/))

This is an operational cloud platform and a useful example of cloud-based railway data services. It should not be counted as evidence that vital train-control logic has moved to the cloud.

#### Wuhan Metro and Huawei

Wuhan Metro Group and Huawei signed a strategic cooperation agreement on 14 May 2020 covering 5G, big data, IoT, AI, and cloud computing. Huawei describes the resulting program as China’s first urban-rail cloud deployed across a multi-line network. Its stated objectives included breaking data silos, integrating more than 20 previously independent service systems, reducing station equipment-room construction costs by half, reducing labor force by more than 10%, and improving IT-resource utilization by approximately 50%. These are case-study claims rather than independently audited lifecycle results. ([Huawei Wuhan Metro case study](https://e.huawei.com/en/case-studies/industries/railway/2023-wuhan-metro))

The communications part of the program is more specific. Wuhan Metro, China Mobile, and Huawei established a 5G-powered Smart Urban Rail Joint Innovation Lab in 2020. By the end of 2021, 5G coverage was reported across all 11 Wuhan Metro lines. The lab verified integrated bearers for CBTC, passenger information systems, train control and management systems, emergency video intercom, and 5G trunking using private-network and slicing technologies. Huawei later reported a 4.9 GHz private network and first-section test results of 101 Mbit/s uplink and 1067 Mbit/s downlink. The evidence demonstrates communications integration and network deployment; it does not show that the CBTC safety logic itself was cloud-hosted. ([Wuhan Metro 5G and cloud case](https://e.huawei.com/en/case-studies/industries/railway/2023-wuhan-metro))

Wuhan also illustrates the difference between a cloud platform procurement and a signaling procurement. In August 2021, Wuhan Metro issued a tender for a line-network informationization cloud platform, disaster-recovery and test systems, information sharing, security, desktop cloud, and control-center-related infrastructure. A November 2021 candidate-winner notice named a Wuhan Fiberhome–Huawei consortium for one lot at approximately CNY 419.69 million and Wuhan Fiberhome for another at approximately CNY 246.00 million. The supplied procurement account does not identify either lot as cloud-CBTC or as a safety-certified train-control deployment. ([Wuhan Metro cloud-platform procurement account](https://cloud.tencent.com.cn/developer/article/1959229?policyId=1003))

Huawei’s later Urban Rail Cloud Platform offering integrates cloud, AI, big data, IoT, video, GIS, integrated communications, intelligent operations centers, smart passenger transport, construction, and O&M. Huawei reports more than 40 partners, four joint innovation laboratories, 72 service systems, and more than 1,000 service indicators in its platform ecosystem. Those figures describe a vendor platform and data ecosystem, not the deployment status of cloud-hosted vital control. ([Huawei Urban Rail Cloud Platform](https://e.huawei.com/en/industries/urban-rail/urban-rail-cloud-platform))

#### Mumbai Metro Line 3: field-tested 5G cloud infrastructure

A July–August 2026 paper reports a proof-of-concept 5G Standalone Captive Non-Public Network on Section 1 of Mumbai Metro Line 3. The project involved Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation Limited, Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited, delaPlex, and VVDN Technologies. It used 3GPP band n78, an O-RAN Option 7.2a split, x86-based CU/DU processing, Indian-manufactured 4T4R radio units, a containerized cloud-native 5G core in a micro data center at the Aarey Operations Control Centre, and passive 1:6 wavelength-division multiplexing. The physical scope was one 1.24 km section, two underground stations, a depot and the intervening tunnel. ([Mumbai Metro Line 3 5G-SA CNPN study](https://www.ijfmr.com/papers/2026/4/85587.pdf))

Acceptance and user-acceptance testing covered five operational domains, including in-motion measurements on revenue-configuration rolling stock. The paper reports:

- Station downlink throughput between 113.00 and 132.00 Mbps.
- Tunnel downlink throughput between 124.17 and 133.26 Mbps.
- Round-trip latency between 16 and 25 ms.
- Uninterrupted session continuity at inter-cell transitions.
- Three concurrently instantiated slices for operational control, video surveillance, and commercial passenger traffic.
- A projected 40–50% capital-expenditure reduction compared with cable-intensive alternatives.

The operational-control slice included CBTC signaling backhaul and ATS telemetry as an engineering service class, with a target of 1–2 Mbps per train and availability of 99.99% or higher. The paper expressly identifies those rate figures as engineering targets, not measured offered load. It also states that it does not claim that live train-control signaling was conveyed and does not establish availability, handover-success distributions, long-term failure rates, or safety certification. The result is therefore strong evidence for a field-tested communications and cloud-native network architecture, not for a qualified cloud-CBTC control system.

The economic figure illustrates the value of a proxy. A projected 40–50% reduction measures a communications-infrastructure comparison over a small underground section; it does not measure the lifecycle cost of cloud-hosted ATP, ZC, CI, and VOBC against a conventional CBTC baseline.

#### Private 5G CBTC and communications overlays

CAF’s signaling division and Cellnex Telecom reported laboratory and field validation of CAF’s OPTIO CBTC over a Cellnex-managed private 5G network in November 2025. They described it as one of the first demonstrations of effective CBTC operation over private 5G. The supplied announcement does not identify the deployment location, a revenue operator, routine commercial operation, cloud-hosted control logic, or a completed safety certification. ([CAF and Cellnex private-5G validation](https://www.cellnex.com/app/uploads/2025/11/11.13.2025_CAF-and-Cellnex-private-5G-network.pdf))

Hitachi Rail has described two related projects. In New York, it is implementing a private 5G network with SelTrac CBTC on the Crosstown Line, reported as carrying approximately 70,000 passengers daily. In Hong Kong, it is implementing a 5G overlay alongside the existing 2.4 GHz radio access network for the Hong Kong International Airport Automated People Mover, which has used SelTrac CBTC since 2012. The supplied account does not identify the New York operating authority or provide completed performance data. ([Hitachi Rail 5G CBTC projects](https://www.masstransitmag.com/rail/railroad-signals-ptc-control-systems-and-products/article/55141473/hitachi-rail-integrates-cbtc-with-5g-begins-development-of-next-gen-rail-battery-through-public-private-partnership))

The Hong Kong presentation provides a detailed private-network security design. CBTC traffic is not routable to the internet or public 5G; it uses static IP addresses, dedicated APNs, 5QI quality-of-service treatment, IPSec tunneling, an intrusion-prevention firewall, and a public-key infrastructure for communication-gateway certificates. The project’s stated concern is preserving GoA4 and SIL4 certification while introducing the new radio layer. Its challenges included tunnel blind spots, security and performance integration, and cut-in without disrupting daily service. This is valuable evidence of how an existing operational CBTC system can introduce a new communications bearer, but it is a communications-overlay modernization, not a cloud-control deployment. ([HKIA APM 5G security presentation](https://irsc2025.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/IRSC-2025-Securing-CBTC-on-HKIA-APM-with-5G_video_Final.pdf))

#### FRMCS and 5GRAIL

FRMCS is the planned successor to GSM-R for railway mobile communications. It combines 3GPP 5G with Mission Critical Services, including mission-critical voice, data, and video. The 5GRAIL field trials used testbeds operated by Deutsche Bahn in Germany and SNCF in France. A six-week campaign integrated prototypes into rolling stock and railway environments, testing communications applications, handovers, video, and simulated ETCS, ATO, and TCMS services. The report states that many prototypes remained at an early development stage. ([5GRAIL field-trial report](https://5grail.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/D5.3-Conclusion-Report-on-5G-FRMCS-Field-Trials.pdf))

The Germany testbed measured mean inter-gNB handover execution at 125 ms in the field compared with 79 ms in the laboratory. The report treats this as an upper bound for user-plane interruption and expects the actual interruption to be lower by some tens of milliseconds. These are handover measurements, not end-to-end cloud-control latency. The France testbed used a suburban line near Paris with 5G standalone at 1.9 GHz over three radio sites; the German testbed used 3.7 GHz over seven sites. Their different radio environments and test objectives prevent direct aggregation.

The Digital Railway Test Field in Germany’s Ore Mountains adds another field-tested enabling environment. Digitale Schiene Deutschland describes an eight-site, 10 km FRMCS test network, with Nokia providing 5G and Kontron Transportation implementing Mission Critical Services. A related proof-of-concept used a 24 km testbed with a 10 km equipped section and an ICE laboratory train. This work demonstrates railway communications virtualization and FRMCS testing, not production urban cloud-CBTC. ([Digitale Schiene Deutschland FRMCS test field](https://digitale-schiene-deutschland.de/en/projects/FRMCS-5G); [FRMCS MCX field evaluation](http://5grail.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Field-Evaluation-of-MCX-Implementations-for-FRMCS.pdf))

### Research and proposed architectures

Several research lines directly address cloud-hosted train control, but they remain proposals, models, or simulations.

#### Software-Defined Train Control

Chang and colleagues’ 2022 SDTC paper proposes moving the logical functions of the onboard controller, zone controller, and interlocking into a cloud platform while leaving sensors and input-output units on the train and wayside. The proposed cloud components include a controller in cloud for each train, a line resource manager, a train registration and allocation controller, and multi-I/O and wayside-I/O units. This is a much more radical change than simply virtualizing ATS or interlocking because the train’s core protection logic would depend on the train-to-cloud path. ([SDTC architecture and reliability evaluation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40864-022-00165-y))

The paper proposes hypervisor-separated virtual machines, multicore commercial servers, software encoding, diverse processors or operating systems, 2oo2 voting, and shared warm-standby servers. It cites a 3GPP Release 16 train-control scenario with less than 100 ms end-to-end transmission delay and 99.9999% reliability as a communications reference. The paper explicitly concludes that SDTC remains conceptual and requires research and testing on wireless performance, 5G suitability, safe-cloud techniques, CPU isolation, diverse software coding, and safe-clock synchronization.

Its reliability comparison is a model rather than a field result. For an assumed 30-train line, the paper estimates MTBF of 8,870.56 hours for SDTC compared with 6,398.14 hours for conventional CBTC—approximately a 39% improvement—and MTTR of 0.86 hours compared with 0.95 hours. It says availability is only slightly better because conventional CBTC already includes substantial redundancy. The calculation assumes particular CASCO parameters, a three-year server MTBF, a common-cause coefficient of 0.01, and 0.01-hour warm-standby activation and repair. It shows how a cloud architecture might change the reliability model; it does not validate those values in operation.

#### ECCBTC and safe cloud-edge control

A 2023 Urban Mass Transit paper proposes ECCBTC, or CBTC based on cloud-edge collaboration, for large-scale urban rail networks. Its three named technologies are a real-time safety cluster, a safety edge controller, and a low-latency, high-determinism communications network. The architecture includes proposed 2oo2 and 2oo3 safety-cloud configurations and claims higher availability, maintainability, and safety, along with lower reconstruction and O&M costs. Those are qualitative design conclusions; the source reports no operational deployment or certification. ([ECCBTC proposal](https://umt1998.tongji.edu.cn/article/doi/10.16037/j.1007-869x.2023.07.036))

A 2024 program described by Xiaofeng Zhao discusses ATS cloud standardization, a SIL4 data-center architecture for wayside ATP/ATO and interlocking, onboard ATP/ATO cloud-edge collaboration, and DCS integration for CBTC, FAO, and TACS retrofit projects. It is a feasibility and planned-research program, not a completed safety case or deployment. ([Zhao urban-rail cloud-edge signaling program](https://trid.trb.org/View/2475688))

Zou’s 2025 study argues theoretically that cloud-edge computing could meet SIL4 requirements through elastic computing and distributed redundancy. It identifies three technical challenges: decoupling data from computing units, secure migration, and distributed fault detection. The paper describes a theoretical basis and technical path, not an operator, pilot, or accepted railway system. ([Zou cloud-edge train-control study](https://umt1998.tongji.edu.cn/en/article/doi/10.16037/j.1007-869x.20241491))

#### Cloud ATS and integrated supervision

Cloud ATS is more mature conceptually than cloud-hosted vital train control because ATS is primarily a supervision and dispatching function, although its availability remains operationally important. A 2023 paper describes production and disaster-recovery data centers at the control center and depot, station nodes connected through a backbone ring, and station backup mode when the cloud data center fails. Conventional ATS services are decomposed into seven microservices: universal, application, control, planning, command, interface, and storage services. ([Cloud ATS architecture](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13677-023-00502-x))

The same study proposes proactive reliability-aware recovery using Age of Information, an LSTM-A2C reinforcement-learning agent, pre-launched backups, flow reconfiguration, and state synchronization. Simulations indicate that proactive recovery can reduce interruption compared with reactive recovery, but the extract provides no field deployment and no independently measured recovery percentage. The architecture imposes a resource trade-off: backup services must occupy separate physical nodes and synchronization bandwidth, and one backup per microservice is permitted in the model.

A 2020 ISCS Plus paper likewise proposes cloud and microservice integration for metro weak-current and supervisory systems. In one surveyed control center, the traditional architecture contained 39 weak-current systems and 56 physical servers excluding storage. A design calculation estimated 19 servers for a cloud arrangement and compared a claimed two-minute recovery with a traditional 15–30-minute restart. These are survey and design calculations, not measurements from an operational cloud deployment. Importantly, the paper recommends merging ATS but retaining ATP and CI as separate systems because of their security and real-time requirements. ([ISCS Plus architecture](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40864-020-00138-z))

#### Cloud-edge scheduling, AI, and digital twins

A 2025 cloud-edge MISCS study places edge gateways near monitoring sources to diagnose data, extract features, and screen anomalies before sending higher-value data to a cloud. It uses Kubernetes, KubeEdge, and a cloud-edge data channel. Simulation reports 32–45% lower latency than pure-cloud or pure-edge alternatives and 18–27% lower task-timeout rates than comparison schedulers. The modeled workload is metro monitoring and supervision, not safety-critical movement authority. ([Cloud-edge MISCS study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40747-025-01969-8))

Research on autonomous control is further from deployment. A 2022 GLOBECOM paper places one edge server per rail line, uses model-predictive control at the edge, and uses deep learning for train-trajectory prediction. Its evidence is extensive simulation. Other studies use mobile-edge computing, multi-hop train-to-train communications, reinforcement learning, or generative AI for virtually coupled train sets. These works may improve future operations, but their reported simulations and experiments do not constitute an operational product or safety certification.

Digital twins are also moving into railway testing and management. A 2025 proposal uses cloud and digital twins to generate complex fully automated-operation scenarios, support training and emergency drills, and provide more realistic 3D test environments than traditional CBTC test platforms. A separate 2025 rail-construction platform integrates edge sensing, cloud data fusion, Kafka, Flink, AI models, BIM/GIS, and digital twins. Field tests reported 91.6% passenger-flow prediction accuracy, 98.2% image-recognition accuracy, 280 ms average response latency, and a 27.4% reduction in average construction task time. These results concern construction management, not train-control safety. ([Urban-rail digital-intelligence platform](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-29732-6))

## 3. A representative cloud-based train-control architecture

### Conventional CBTC as the starting point

The conventional arrangement is distributed by design. Vital functions are placed in train-borne controllers, zone controllers, computer interlockings, and other safety computers. The DCS provides redundant paths between them. Local ATS or interlocking functionality can remain available when the central control center is disconnected.

This distribution has costs. A train may contain redundant VOBC equipment; a station area may contain CI, ZC, local ATS, and specialized I/O; and different suppliers may use non-interchangeable boards and interfaces. The 2022 SDTC paper identifies these interfaces and hardware dependencies as a maintenance and expansion problem. But distribution also limits the consequences of a central data-center failure and keeps some safety logic close to the physical equipment.

A cloud architecture does not remove the field layer. Trains still need sensors, braking and traction interfaces, doors, onboard networks, antennas, power, and local diagnostics. Wayside equipment still needs to sense points, signals, track occupancy, platform doors, and other physical conditions. The important design question is which logical functions move, where they run, and what happens when the cloud or communications path is unavailable.

### Four layers of a cloud-edge design

A practical architecture can be described in four layers.

| Layer | Main elements | Typical cloud-edge role | Required protection |
|---|---|---|---|
| Field and vehicle | Sensors, odometry, balises, axle counters, points, platform doors, train interfaces, local I/O | Collect physical state and execute commands | Ruggedization, local diagnostics, safe-state behavior |
| Train-to-ground and backbone network | Private 5G, FRMCS, WLAN, fiber, DCS, TSN, redundant rings | Carry vital and non-vital data with controlled QoS | Dual paths, bounded latency, handover continuity, segmentation |
| Edge and private-cloud compute | Edge servers, micro data centers, control-center and disaster-recovery data centers | Host selected ATS, interlocking, ZC, VOBC, analytics, and orchestration functions | SIL architecture, isolation, voting, failover, time synchronization |
| Application and management plane | ATS, ATO, ATP, CI, ZC, digital twins, data platforms, O&M, security monitoring | Coordinate operations and analyze system state | Certified interfaces, access control, logging, configuration discipline |

The resulting control path can be summarized as:

`Train and wayside sensors → redundant wireless/DCS → edge or private data center → vital control logic → redundant return path → train and wayside actuators`

A monitoring path is different:

`Sensors and equipment → edge filtering → cloud data platform → analytics/digital twin/maintenance application`

The second path can tolerate more delay, buffering, and temporary disconnection than the first. Treating both as one “cloud railway” obscures the assurance problem.

### Control-function placement

There are at least four possible placement strategies.

#### Cloud ATS and supervision first

The least disruptive approach moves timetable management, visualization, alarm handling, maintenance data, and non-vital supervision into a private cloud while retaining ATP, ZC, CI, and VOBC in conventional locations. The 2023 ATS architecture follows this general pattern: cloud services remain connected to station nodes, and stations switch to backup mode after a data-center failure.

This produces many of the early benefits—shared servers, centralized data, easier application expansion, and common monitoring—without placing movement authority directly across a cloud network.

#### Cloud interlocking with local I/O

The next step virtualizes interlocking logic while keeping point machines, signals, platform doors, and other field I/O at the wayside. Siemens DS3 and Signaling X are examples of this direction. The safety logic runs in a private data center, while the field layer remains physically distributed.

This can reduce station equipment and permit COTS hardware refresh, but the control path still depends on communication between the data center and wayside I/O. Geographic redundancy and local fallback become essential.

#### Cloud or edge ZC and VOBC logic

The SDTC proposal is more ambitious. It places the logical functions of the VOBC, ZC, and CI in a cloud, leaving sensors and I/O on trains and along the track. The train sends speed and location information to a cloud controller and receives braking, traction, and door commands.

This arrangement maximizes software reuse and makes generic cloud resources available to many trains. It also makes wireless performance, timing, state consistency, safe failover, and cyber protection central parts of the train-control safety case. The supplied research explicitly treats this as conceptual.

#### Hybrid cloud-edge-end control

A likely intermediate architecture keeps the most time-sensitive or failure-critical functions on the train or at a nearby edge node, while using a central cloud for coordination, optimization, data management, simulation, and less time-sensitive logic. The edge may be located at a station, depot, line control center, or micro data center. The central cloud can manage multiple lines and provide common services.

This is the logic behind ECCBTC, cloud-edge MISCS, and several 5G-MEC proposals. It does not eliminate cloud dependence, but it can reduce the distance and queuing exposure of a local control loop.

### Latency is a chain, not a single cloud number

A cloud-control path has multiple timing components:

$`T_{\mathrm{e2e}}=T_{\mathrm{wireless,up}}+T_{\mathrm{transport,up}}+T_{\mathrm{queue}}+T_{\mathrm{compute}}+T_{\mathrm{transport,down}}+T_{\mathrm{wireless,down}}+T_{\mathrm{I/O}}`$

The relevant quantity is not the average application response time of a cloud dashboard. It is the worst-case or high-percentile delay and its behavior during handover, congestion, retransmission, data-center failure, time-sync loss, and cyberattack.

Edge placement reduces transport distance and may remove a central queue. A local user-plane function in the Mumbai Metro Line 3 architecture is intended to provide a shorter path for station-local traffic, but the paper does not measure a safety-critical CBTC loop. Similarly, the 16–25 ms round-trip results reported for the Mumbai network demonstrate a communications bearer under the tested conditions; they do not establish the latency distribution of a complete cloud movement-authority loop.

### Migration and coexistence

A cloud deployment normally has to coexist with legacy trains, wayside equipment, radio systems, interlockings, and operational procedures. The transition may require:

- Gateways between old and new interfaces.
- Dual radio or dual network operation.
- Compatibility with legacy VOBC and TCMS equipment.
- Wayside I/O replacement or adaptation.
- Separate test, shadow, and operational modes.
- Repeated safety analysis for changed interfaces and failure assumptions.
- Cutover procedures that preserve service and rollback capability.
- New control-center, maintenance, and cyber-monitoring responsibilities.

The TSTCBTC 2.0 account claims a seamless old-to-new signaling cutover on Shanghai Metro Line 5, but that was a conventional CBTC modernization, not a cloud migration. BART’s program illustrates the broader scale of railway signaling modernization: test-track validation, staged geographic deployment, cable replacement, field surveys, and construction support. Cloud architecture can reduce some hardware replacement, but it cannot bypass the physical and organizational migration boundary.

## 4. Key enabling technologies

### Virtualization, COTS servers, containers, and microservices

Virtualization separates an application from the physical server. A hypervisor can allocate processor cores, memory, and interfaces to virtual machines, while containers package applications and their dependencies with less overhead. Kubernetes and related platforms orchestrate containers, restart failed services, move workloads, and manage scaling.

For ordinary urban-rail cloud services, these technologies offer clear advantages:

- Several lines or subsystems can share a server pool.
- Computing capacity can be allocated according to demand.
- Applications can be expanded independently.
- Hardware can be replaced without redesigning every application.
- Software updates and configuration can be managed centrally.
- A backup instance can be created on a different physical node.

The 2023 cloud ATS architecture decomposes ATS into seven microservices and uses load balancing and independent service extension. The 2025 MISCS platform uses Kubernetes and KubeEdge to coordinate cloud and edge containers. These are credible cloud-native patterns for supervision, monitoring, and data processing.

Vital control introduces stricter constraints. A safety assessor must establish freedom from interference between applications, predictable execution time, memory and processor isolation, deterministic communication, secure boot and software provenance, controlled configuration, and behavior during partial failure. A 2022 Railway Signaling as a Service paper identifies temporal isolation in general-purpose hypervisors as a problem relevant to EN 50128 certification. ([Railway Signaling as a Service](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2208.14109))

Containers are not automatically safe or unsafe. Their suitability depends on the complete platform: kernel, hypervisor, hardware, operating system, orchestration, network, monitoring, update policy, and safety architecture. A cloud platform that elastically moves ordinary applications cannot simply be assumed to preserve the timing and independence required by a SIL4 function.

### Private cloud and data-center design

The safety-oriented cloud model is usually a private cloud under the operator’s or infrastructure manager’s control. It may consist of:

- A primary operations-control data center.
- A geographically separated disaster-recovery or backup center.
- Edge or station data centers.
- Redundant network paths.
- Independent power, cooling, fire protection, and physical access controls.
- A controlled software and configuration repository.
- Local station fallback equipment.

The ATS study places production and disaster-recovery centers at the control center and depot and gives station nodes a backup mode. Siemens describes DS3 as using independent servers and geographic redundancy. The proposed SDTC architecture similarly allows cloud centers at the control center and backup center.

The cloud is therefore not just a remote server room. It is a distributed safety and availability system. Geographic separation reduces a single-site failure but increases the need for state consistency, clock alignment, wide-area communications, and disciplined failover. A second site that has stale or inconsistent movement-authority state is not a safe backup merely because it is geographically distant.

### Edge computing

Edge computing places processing close to the data source or control endpoint. In metro systems, an edge node may be located at a station, depot, line control room, radio-access site, or micro data center.

Edge computing addresses three limitations of a centralized cloud:

1. It reduces transmission distance and round-trip delay.
2. It reduces the volume of raw data sent to the central cloud.
3. It allows local action or fallback during a backhaul interruption.

The MISCS paper describes edge nodes that perform diagnosis, feature extraction, anomaly screening, and data reduction before sending high-value data to the cloud. Its simulation reports a 32–45% latency reduction compared with pure edge or pure cloud alternatives, but the modeled application is monitoring rather than vital train control.

The Mumbai Metro Line 3 architecture demonstrates a related physical pattern: a cloud-native 5G core in a micro data center and distributed network functions intended to keep communications close to the metro estate. Its measured 16–25 ms round-trip results are useful for communications engineering, but the source does not establish the response of a complete safety-control application.

For cloud-CBTC, edge computing is likely to be important even if the long-term objective is centralized software. The cloud can coordinate lines and maintain common services, while edge nodes handle local I/O, local protection, data filtering, and fallback. The unresolved question is how much vital logic can be placed at the edge without recreating the hardware and maintenance fragmentation that cloud architecture is meant to reduce.

### 5G, private railway wireless, and FRMCS

#### Why 5G is relevant

CBTC needs a continuous train-to-ground bearer with mobility, coverage, low packet loss, predictable latency, and rapid handover. 5G contributes:

- Flexible uplink and downlink allocation.
- Higher capacity than many legacy railway radios.
- Standalone cores and private network deployment.
- Quality-of-service classes and network slicing.
- Mobile-edge computing.
- Mission-critical voice, data, and video.
- Integration with time-sensitive networking.
- Potentially more convenient support for multiple rail subsystems.

ZTE’s 2025 overview describes 5G network slicing as multiple logical end-to-end networks across shared physical infrastructure, with isolation across equipment, access, transport, and core domains. It also describes 5G MEC for video AI, depot inspection, catenary detection, positioning, and passenger-flow analysis. These are important operational capabilities, but network slicing alone is not a safety certificate.

#### Private networks versus public networks

The evidence favors private or tightly controlled railway networks for safety-relevant traffic. The Hong Kong APM design keeps CBTC traffic off the public internet and uses dedicated APNs, quality-of-service treatment, IPSec, firewalls, and certificates. The Mumbai project used a captive non-public network with a cloud-native core inside the metro estate. Siemens describes its Signaling Data Center as operator-controlled.

Carrier 5G can still be valuable. Huawei’s Wuhan account reports that carrier networks along many metro lines had physical-resource-block utilization of approximately 20% because passenger demand is tidal. It proposes using idle capacity for quasi-real-time or off-peak metro services. The same account says Wuhan’s procurement decision emphasized reliability, availability, security, and data redundancy rather than price. It also describes private-network construction as costing more than CNY 1 million per kilometer of track in some traditional metro deployments, while carrier leasing could have a roughly similar total cost. These figures are an industry business-model comparison, not a controlled CBTC cost study. ([Huawei Wuhan 5G business-model account](https://www.huawei.com/en/huaweitech/publication/202401/5g-smart-urban-rail-wuhan))

#### Latency targets are not interchangeable

A 2022 SDTC paper cites a 3GPP Release 16 train-control scenario with end-to-end transmission delay below 100 ms and reliability of 99.9999%. Cisco’s general CBTC guidance gives design targets below 500 ms network latency, below 50 ms handover time, and below 0.1% packet loss. ZTE reports a vendor capability of 10 ± 1 ms for a 5G-TSN deterministic service. A 2024 industrial 5G-TSN experiment measured approximately 10 ms average round-trip latency. These numbers describe different systems, definitions, traffic, and test conditions. They cannot be ranked as if they were measurements of the same CBTC control loop.

The 5GRAIL field trial illustrates why handover requires separate treatment: the German testbed measured 125 ms mean handover execution in the field and 79 ms in the laboratory, while the report noted that user-plane interruption could be lower than execution time. The Mumbai paper reported 16–25 ms round-trip latency for a particular communications test. Neither result establishes a complete cloud-CBTC worst-case latency distribution.

#### FRMCS and mission-critical services

FRMCS is designed to provide a standardized mobile communications platform for railway operations as GSM-R is eventually supplemented and replaced. Its 3GPP Mission Critical Services layer includes MCPTT, MCData, and MCVideo, together with authentication, authorization, quality-of-service handling, location services, and end-to-end security. FRMCS field trials demonstrate a promising railway communications foundation, but standardization and verification remain evolutionary, and the supplied trials do not establish production urban cloud-CBTC.

### Deterministic networking and time synchronization

Average latency is not the same as deterministic latency. A control system needs predictable delivery, bounded jitter, known packet-loss behavior, and synchronized clocks.

Time-sensitive networking provides a relevant technology stack:

- IEEE 802.1AS provides time synchronization based on the Precision Time Protocol family.
- IEEE 802.1CB provides frame replication and elimination for reliability.
- IEEE 802.1Qcc supports stream and resource configuration.
- IEEE 802.1Qbv uses time-aware gates and schedules traffic in transmit windows.
- 3GPP Releases 16 and later define mechanisms for integrating 5G with TSN, including translators, time-sensitive communication functions, hold-and-forward buffering, and uplink synchronization.

In a TSN network, a global clock and gate-control list determine when a queue can transmit. Clock drift can misalign the schedule and add latency. The TSN study reports that a hybrid 5G/TSN testbed achieved approximately 10 ms average round-trip latency, but its vanilla 5G system behaved less deterministically when the TSN schedule became stringent. At 200 ms and 100 ms base periods, traffic retained periodicity. At 50 ms and 40 ms periods, the experiment observed non-strict periodicity and possible packet delays or losses. The authors conclude that end-to-end optimization, TSN-aware 5G scheduling, tight synchronization, and a global schedule are necessary. ([5G and TSN testbed](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.05989v1))

The experiment was industrial rather than railway-specific, but the mechanism is directly relevant. A 5G radio network with good average latency is not automatically a deterministic train-control network. The schedule, synchronization, retransmission behavior, radio handover, queueing, and failure recovery all have to be engineered together.

Railway cloud research also identifies RaSTA, DDS, OPC UA Safety, One Channel Safe, and separation-kernel communication architectures as candidate technologies. The SIL4 Cloud report describes these as subjects for comparison and early-stage research, not as a complete field-validated protocol stack. ([SIL4 Cloud report](https://digitale-schiene-deutschland.de/Downloads/Report%20-%20SIL4%20Cloud.pdf))

### IoT and data platforms

IoT platforms provide the data fabric around train control. They connect sensors, equipment, video, energy systems, passenger flows, maintenance records, and operational logs. Common technologies include MQTT, OPC UA, Kafka, Flink, time-series databases, graph databases, object storage, schema registries, and API gateways.

The rail-construction platform described in *Scientific Reports* uses edge sensing, Kafka and Flink stream processing, BIM/GIS, distributed databases, AI inference, and digital twins. The cloud-edge MISCS paper uses edge gateways to reduce redundant data and send refined information to the cloud. Huawei’s urban-rail cloud programs similarly emphasize breaking data silos across multiple service systems.

These technologies improve visibility and support preventive maintenance, but they should remain logically separated from the vital movement-authority path unless they are independently assessed for that role. A video analytics pipeline can be cloud-native and highly available without being suitable for controlling a brake command.

### AI and machine learning

AI is already useful around train control, but its strongest evidence is supervisory rather than vital.

Current or near-term uses include:

- Predictive maintenance for rolling stock, track, catenary, points, and signaling equipment.
- Detection of abnormal equipment states.
- Passenger-flow prediction and crowd management.
- Timetable and resource optimization.
- Incident classification and response support.
- Network capacity and energy optimization.
- Failure prediction for cloud microservices.
- Digital-twin scenario generation and test automation.
- Remote inspection and video analytics.

The cloud ATS recovery study uses LSTM-A2C to classify ordinary, alert, and critical microservice states and decide when to launch backups or synchronize state. In simulation, the LSTM-A2C model correctly handled approximately 92% of critical-state actions and placed backups in the alert state approximately 68% of the time. These are simulation results from a modeled ATS cloud, not field measurements.

The 2026 cyber-physical risk-modeling paper applies complex-network, fault-tree, attack-graph, and SARSA methods to a cloud-CBTC model. It identifies a modeled physical master node with degree 36.14 as especially critical and reports a modeled risk reduction from 85.4 to 31.2 after security measures. The 63.5% reduction is an application-verification result in the model, not an operational metro outcome. ([Cloud-CBTC risk model](https://doi.org/10.20532/cit.2026.1006258))

AI in the vital control loop presents additional assurance problems:

- Training data may not cover rare failures or unusual operating conditions.
- The model may change as data or parameters change.
- It may be difficult to demonstrate exhaustive behavior.
- A prediction confidence score is not the same as a safety proof.
- An adversarial or corrupted input can produce unsafe recommendations.
- Human operators may misunderstand or over-trust an opaque output.
- A safety filter may constrain an AI command but does not automatically certify the combined system.

For these reasons, AI is most defensible today as a monitoring, prediction, optimization, or advisory layer with deterministic safeguards and human or certified-system confirmation. The supplied evidence does not show independently certified AI as the movement-authority controller of an urban CBTC system.

### Digital twins

A digital twin is a continuously updated virtual representation of a physical asset or process, connected through bidirectional data exchange. In railway applications, digital twins can represent rolling stock, stations, infrastructure, signaling equipment, passenger flows, and operational states. A 2023 railway digital-twin review describes uses in asset monitoring, train-movement supervision, failure prediction, and maintenance, while noting that standardized definitions and implementation architectures remain incomplete. ([Railway digital-twin review](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40860-023-00208-6))

For cloud-based train control, digital twins can support:

- Factory and site acceptance testing.
- Shadow operation before cutover.
- Replay of incidents and degraded modes.
- Driverless-operation and emergency-drill scenarios.
- Training for dispatchers and maintainers.
- Validation of migration and timetable changes.
- Predictive maintenance and asset-health management.
- Evaluation of proposed AI strategies without directly controlling trains.

The 2025 UTO/FAO test-platform proposal uses cloud computing, 3D rendering, and simulation to create complex scenarios for testing and training. The 2025 rail-construction platform uses BIM/GIS, AI, and digital twins in a closed-loop construction-management application. Both demonstrate the value of digital twins around railway operations. Neither establishes a certified digital twin as the direct safety authority for train movement.

### Redundancy, voting, and failover

Cloud systems can use redundancy more flexibly than physically isolated conventional systems, but redundancy must be designed at several levels.

#### Hardware and execution redundancy

A 2oo2 architecture requires two channels to agree before a safety output is accepted. A 2oo3 architecture can tolerate a disagreement or one failed channel while maintaining a majority decision. The proposed ECCBTC architecture discusses both. A 3oo5 architecture, described in a 2026 railway-signaling cloud design source, uses five nodes, requires at least three available nodes, and can tolerate two failed nodes under a weighted-voting and monitoring-arbitration scheme. The source provides a design specification, not a completed deployment. ([Railway signaling cloud redundancy architecture](http://www.cssjj.com.cn/EN/10.16265/j.cnki.issn1003-3033.2026.06.0794))

#### Hot and warm standby

A hot standby continuously maintains the state needed to take over rapidly. A warm standby may have the correct software and configuration but require activation and state restoration. Cloud architectures can use generic warm-standby servers for several applications rather than purchasing a dedicated backup machine for each physically isolated subsystem.

This is one of the strongest theoretical advantages of cloud computing. It is also a source of risk. The standby must have current and trustworthy state, the orchestration system must not create a split-brain condition, the failover decision must be safe, and the transition must remain within the permitted operational window.

#### Geographic redundancy

Separate data centers reduce exposure to fire, flooding, power loss, equipment-room failure, or a local network cut. They also create a larger synchronization problem. A railway cannot safely switch to a remote center unless that center has an authoritative view of train positions, route reservations, points, temporary speed restrictions, and current movement authorities.

#### Local fallback

The 2023 cloud ATS design uses station backup mode after data-center failure. A complete cloud-CBTC design would need a defined local fallback or restrictive safe state for loss of the cloud, network, time reference, or data integrity. The exact fallback could be local ATP, station interlocking, restricted manual operation, emergency braking, or another approved degraded mode. The important point is that the behavior must be specified, tested, and included in the safety case; it cannot be left to the cloud orchestrator’s normal restart logic.

## 5. Safety, reliability, cybersecurity, and standards

### Safety integrity is a system property

Safety Integrity Level, or SIL, expresses the rigor and safety integrity required of a function. SIL4 is the highest railway level commonly cited for functions whose dangerous failure could have catastrophic consequences. In the Siemens DS3 account, SIL4 is associated with a tolerable hazard rate better than $`10^{-9}`$ per hour per function. The number is a target for dangerous failure probability, not a guarantee that every component of a cloud architecture is SIL4.

A safety case must connect:

- Hazard identification and risk acceptance.
- System architecture and independence.
- Hardware random-failure analysis.
- Software development and verification.
- Communication integrity and availability.
- Timing and synchronization.
- Fail-safe output behavior.
- Common-cause and systematic failures.
- Cybersecurity effects on functional safety.
- Maintenance, configuration, upgrades, and operating procedures.
- Independent assessment and authority acceptance.

A SIL4-certified execution platform is therefore not equivalent to a SIL4-certified urban cloud-CBTC deployment. DS3’s Achau result is an important platform and interlocking reference. The Rostock trial must still demonstrate the complete application, interfaces, operating conditions, and local acceptance requirements for its specific urban environment.

### Functional-safety standards

The principal railway safety standards have different scopes.

| Standard or framework | Main scope | Relevance to cloud-based train control |
|---|---|---|
| EN 50126 / IEC 62278 | Reliability, availability, maintainability, and safety lifecycle | Requires RAMS analysis across the railway lifecycle, including cloud infrastructure and migration assumptions |
| EN 50128 / IEC 62279 | Software for railway control and protection | Applies to safety-related software, including virtualized execution, tools, updates, and timing assumptions |
| EN 50129 / IEC 62425 | Safety-related electronic signaling systems and safety cases | Requires evidence that the specific safety function and SIL are acceptable |
| IEEE 1474.1 | CBTC performance and functional requirements | Defines CBTC functions, communications, localization, and ATP-related requirements |
| IEC 62290-2:2025 | Urban guided transport management and command/control, GOA1–GOA4 | Provides functional requirements for new and upgraded urban guided transport systems but does not specifically address security |
| IEC 62443 | Industrial automation and control cybersecurity | Provides zones, conduits, security levels, and roles for asset owners, integrators, and suppliers |
| CLC/TS 50701 | Railway cybersecurity | Applies railway-specific cybersecurity lifecycle and zoning principles |
| IEC 63452 | Security and safety-related urban-rail guidance in relevant jurisdictions | Provides an additional voluntary or locally specified framework; acceptance remains authority-specific |
| 3GPP, IEEE TSN, and ITU-T timing standards | Wireless, QoS, synchronization, and deterministic networking | Define communications capabilities and constraints, not the railway safety case by themselves |

DNV maps EN 50126 to RAMS, EN 50128 to railway-control software, and EN 50129 to safety-related electronic signaling. ([DNV functional-safety overview](https://www.dnv.us/services/functional-safety-for-rail-industry-82739/))

IEC 62425:2025, the second edition of the railway signaling functional-safety standard, is especially relevant to cloud migration. It adds guidance on reuse of pre-existing systems, safety-related tools, the impact of cybersecurity threats on functional safety, and specific application safety cases. It also provides a dedicated safety-case structure. At the same time, the standard states that cybersecurity aspects of functional safety are addressed only to a limited extent; it is not a complete cybersecurity standard. ([IEC 62425:2025 scope](https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/68909); [IEC revision summary](https://cdn.standards.iteh.ai/samples/iec/iec-62425-2025/e82819bfbf514761830a56b4cb44c4a0/iec-62425-2025.pdf))

IEC 62290-2:2025 covers urban guided transport systems from GoA1 through GoA4 and can support new lines and upgrades. It explicitly states that the IEC 62290 series does not specifically address security, so a cloud-CBTC program needs additional cybersecurity engineering. ([IEC 62290-2:2025](https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/83774))

### Reliability and availability

Reliability and availability are related but not identical. A system may have a high mean time between failures but a poor service outcome if repairs are slow. A common availability expression is:

$`A=\frac{\mathrm{MTBF}}{\mathrm{MTBF}+\mathrm{MTTR}}`$

Cloud architectures can improve MTTR through automated restart, virtual-machine migration, shared standby capacity, and centralized maintenance. They can also reduce hardware variety and spare-parts requirements. The same mechanisms can create new common modes: a faulty software update, orchestration error, shared storage failure, time-service failure, or compromised management plane may affect many nominally redundant applications at once.

The SDTC paper’s Markov model illustrates both sides. It estimates an MTBF improvement of approximately 39% and a roughly 10% MTTR reduction, while finding only a slight availability improvement because conventional CBTC already contains considerable redundancy. The model assumes parameters rather than measuring a field system. Its most favorable result concerns cloud CiC redundancy, where generic standby servers can serve multiple virtual functions; that is a design advantage, not an observed urban-rail operating statistic.

The cloud ATS research uses proactive failure prediction and Age of Information to pre-launch backups before a service becomes critical. This addresses the difference between reactive recovery, which starts after failure, and proactive recovery, which consumes resources in advance to reduce interruption. The trade-off is explicit: ordinary-state backups can waste resources, while critical-state services need fresher synchronization and more protection. The paper reports simulation evidence, not an operational availability figure.

A complete cloud-CBTC reliability case would need to measure at least:

- Availability of the train-to-ground communication path.
- Packet loss and retransmission behavior.
- Handover interruption and re-establishment.
- Primary-to-secondary data-center transfer.
- State synchronization delay and correctness.
- Local fallback behavior.
- Common-cause failure in hardware, software, power, timing, and cyber controls.
- Performance under maximum train density and passenger-service load.
- Recovery after deliberate denial-of-service and radio-jamming conditions.

Those results are not supplied for a complete urban cloud-CBTC system.

### Fail-safe behavior

CBTC’s central safety purpose is to prevent collisions, overspeed, unsafe separation, and conflicting routes. Cisco describes ATP as enforcing permitted speed and applying brakes if needed, while interlocking prevents conflicting movements. A cloud design must preserve that safety intent when data are missing, stale, contradictory, delayed, or malicious.

Safe behavior may require:

- Rejecting stale or unauthenticated train-position data.
- Withholding a new movement authority when required state is unavailable.
- Applying a restrictive speed or braking profile.
- Preventing a route command when point or occupancy status is uncertain.
- Switching to local or station-based backup.
- Separating control and monitoring traffic.
- Recording the event for investigation and recovery.

The exact implementation depends on the system and authority. It should not be inferred from the presence of redundancy or a cloud platform. A redundant system that reaches an incorrect consensus, or a failover system that uses stale state, can be highly available without being safe.

### Cybersecurity threats introduced or amplified by cloud architecture

Cloud migration changes the threat model in several ways.

#### Expanded attack surface

COTS servers, hypervisors, container registries, orchestration APIs, remote-management tools, standard IP protocols, software repositories, cloud dashboards, and data-center networks create more interfaces than a historically isolated proprietary signaling cabinet.

#### Privileged access and cloud pivoting

A compromised enterprise or maintenance account could attempt to pivot toward the operational cloud. A malicious cloud administrator, exposed management interface, compromised image, or stolen certificate could affect multiple lines or applications. Multi-site deployment can turn a local incident into a regional one if common credentials, software, or orchestration are shared.

#### Availability attacks

A railway attacker does not need to alter a movement authority to disrupt service. Jamming, denial of service, resource exhaustion, cloud control-plane failure, or a deliberate synchronization attack may force trains into restrictive operation. A June 2026 study by researchers at TUM CIT and Fraunhofer AISEC identified jamming, denial-of-service, and data-integrity vulnerabilities associated with legacy GSM-R and EuroBalises. The study also concluded that availability attacks remain insufficiently addressed by current European railway safety standards bodies. ([TUM CIT and Fraunhofer AISEC findings as reported](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/327377/20260911/siemens-runs-cloud-rail-signaling-under-live-german-tram-passengers-innotrans-debut-11-days-out.htm))

#### Integrity and timing attacks

A delayed, replayed, or modified position report can be as dangerous as a lost report. Cloud services also depend on time sources and synchronization. A compromised time service could disrupt scheduled traffic, certificate validation, event ordering, or failover decisions.

#### Supply-chain and software-update risks

COTS hardware and open-source components can reduce vendor lock-in but introduce firmware, operating-system, container-image, and dependency risks. A railway safety patch may require reassessment. A cybersecurity patch cannot simply be applied as it would be to an ordinary enterprise server if it might alter certified behavior.

### Security architecture

An effective architecture needs more than physical isolation. Cisco’s rail guide explicitly warns that air-gapping alone does not prevent attacks and recommends a coordinated approach covering authorized users and devices, access control, malware prevention, legitimate traffic, monitoring, policy enforcement, and rapid response. ([Cisco Rail CBTC and Safety Design Guide](https://www.cisco.com/c/dam/en/us/td/docs/solutions/Verticals/Transportation/Rail-CBTC/Rail_CBTC_Design_Guide.pdf?dtid=odicdc000509))

Relevant controls include:

- Zones and conduits separating safety-related, non-safety, enterprise, passenger, maintenance, and external systems.
- Least privilege and separation of duties.
- Multifactor authentication for privileged access.
- Hardware-rooted identity, certificates, and key rotation.
- Mutual authentication and integrity protection for control messages.
- Strictly filtered and monitored cloud-to-OT commands.
- Unidirectional or tightly controlled OT-to-cloud telemetry where appropriate.
- Independent management and production networks.
- Network slicing combined with physical and logical isolation.
- Passive monitoring of legacy OT protocols.
- Secure boot, signed software, image provenance, and controlled repositories.
- Intrusion detection and anomaly monitoring that do not interfere with certified control behavior.
- Tested incident response and safe degraded operation.
- Offline recovery capability if the central management plane is unavailable.

The UITP/ENISA cloud-security material recommends that control signals from cloud instances to OT be filtered, authenticated, and monitored for anomalies, while non-control telemetry from OT to cloud can be designed as unidirectional. It also recommends strong segmentation and security levels appropriate to systems handling SIL3–SIL4 functions. This material is guidance in a preview presentation, not evidence of field validation. ([UITP/ENISA cloud and safety-critical systems presentation](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-12/session%205-2%20-%20uitp%20-%20securing%20connection%20safety-critical%20systems%20and%20the%20cloud.pdf))

IEC 62443 provides zones, conduits, Security Levels 1–4, and roles for asset owners, integrators, and suppliers. CLC/TS 50701 applies those ideas to railway cybersecurity. The cybersecurity control system must also account for the long life of rail assets: legacy systems may remain in service for decades and may not support modern authentication or patching.

### Certification and acceptance

There is no single global approval path for every urban railway. Acceptance, approval, and certification of non-SERA urban rail systems may be assigned to national, regional, or local authorities. UITP notes that IEC 63452 is voluntary unless local rules specify otherwise, and that the applicability of recent European cybersecurity legislation to non-SERA systems has required clarification. ([UITP safety, security, and cybersecurity report](https://mylibrary.uitp.org/GED_V14/295612401389/Report_-_Safety_Security_Cybersecurity_non-SERA_rail_systems_1501.pdf))

For a cloud-CBTC project, the safety case must address not only the signaling application but also:

- The selected cloud platform and server hardware.
- Hypervisor and operating-system behavior.
- Container or VM isolation.
- Orchestration and service placement.
- Network timing and deterministic behavior.
- Data-center power, cooling, and physical security.
- Primary and backup state consistency.
- Network and wireless failure.
- Cybersecurity threats that could affect safety.
- Configuration and software-update procedures.
- Human operation and maintenance.
- Legacy interfaces and coexistence.
- Evidence from testing under normal and degraded conditions.

The supplied evidence does not show an independent safety case and certification for a complete urban cloud-CBTC deployment covering all of those elements. That is the central remaining assurance gap.

## 6. Cloud-edge control compared with conventional on-premises CBTC

“On-premises” and “cloud” are not exact opposites. A private railway cloud may be physically located at the operator’s control center, depot, or station. The practical distinction is whether safety software is tied to specialized, dedicated hardware and fixed application locations or is decoupled into virtualized services that can be placed, replicated, and refreshed across a managed compute pool.

| Comparison axis | Conventional on-premises CBTC | Cloud or cloud-edge CBTC proposition | Evidence and limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vital function scope | VOBC, ZC, CI, ATS, and DCS are distributed across dedicated train, station, wayside, and control-center equipment | Selected or all logical functions run in private cloud or edge compute, with field I/O retained locally | Full cloud hosting remains proposed or trial-stage; most operational cloud examples are ATS, monitoring, or communications |
