| Latency and determinism | Fixed, engineered paths and local processing can simplify timing analysis | Private 5G, fiber, edge placement, TSN, and slicing can provide controlled paths, but add wireless, queueing, and synchronization dependencies | Measured communications values exist, but no like-for-like complete cloud-CBTC latency dataset exists |
| Availability | Mature duplicated networks, hot standby, local fallback, and dedicated hardware | Geo-redundant data centers, VM migration, pooled warm standby, voting, and software recovery | Cloud may improve MTTR and resource sharing, but creates common cloud, orchestration, timing, and cyber failure modes |
| Scalability | Expansion often requires additional signaling hardware, interfaces, and site work | Virtual machines, containers, shared servers, and microservices can expand by configuration or resource allocation | Elasticity is best demonstrated for supervision and data services; vital scaling remains unvalidated |
| Maintainability | Hardware-specific spares, long vendor lifecycles, and field visits | COTS refresh, centralized monitoring, standardized servers, and software-defined functions | Certified software changes may trigger reassessment; cloud operations require new IT/OT skills |
| Capacity | Headway depends on CBTC algorithms, braking, dwell, route conflicts, and operations | More compute can support larger models, more trains, or network-level optimization | Cloud alone does not create shorter headways; no controlled cloud-versus-conventional capacity result exists |
| Capital and lifecycle cost | Specialized hardware, wayside rooms, cables, and vendor-specific maintenance | Potentially fewer equipment rooms, shared compute, reduced cabling, and lower marginal cost for new services | MML3’s 40–50% figure is a projected communications proxy; vendor efficiency and energy claims lack common baselines |
| Deployment flexibility | Functions are tied to sites and hardware platforms | Software can be placed at a control center, edge node, or backup center and reused across lines | Migration still requires legacy interfaces, vehicle work, testing, safety acceptance, and operational cutover |
| Cybersecurity and assurance | Historically relied more on proprietary protocols and physical isolation | Enables active monitoring and standard security controls but expands IP, virtualization, supply-chain, and remote-access exposure | Private cloud reduces exposure but does not eliminate cloud-specific threats or the need for an independent safety case |

### Latency: locality versus flexibility

A conventional CBTC system often has a shorter and more predictable path between the control function and the physical equipment. Its dedicated DCS can be engineered around fixed station and wayside locations. That does not make it immune to radio loss, congestion, or synchronization failures, but the timing boundary is usually easier to describe.

Cloud control adds at least one network segment between the field device and the logical controller. A private fiber network and a nearby edge center can keep that path short. A central data center serving multiple lines creates more distance, more aggregation, and more potential queueing. Public-network routing would add further uncertainty and is not the model supported by the strongest safety-oriented evidence.

The trade-off is therefore not “cloud is slow” versus “on-premises is fast.” It is whether the cloud-edge architecture can provide a bounded and assured control path under the complete operating envelope. The current evidence includes average or test-condition communications results, but not the required full system distributions under maximum load, handover, failure, and attack.

### Availability: pooled resilience versus shared failure

Conventional CBTC already uses redundancy. Cisco’s reference architecture duplicates the operations center, core, backbone, wayside access, wireless paths, and onboard networks. TSTCBTC 2.0 describes dual CBTC systems, and the 2021 DCS study describes dual networks, ring backbones, and hot backup.

Cloud architecture can pool standby resources and make a generic spare server available to multiple virtual functions. The SDTC model estimates better MTBF and MTTR from this arrangement. A cloud system can also place redundant workloads in geographically separated centers and automate failover.

But virtualization can create a common failure domain. An incorrect image, orchestration bug, storage failure, time-service error, management-plane compromise, or shared network misconfiguration can affect all logical replicas. Conventional physical separation may be inefficient but can provide diversity that is difficult to reproduce in a homogeneous cloud. The safety case must demonstrate independence rather than count virtual machines.

### Scalability and capacity

Cloud computing is naturally scalable for data, monitoring, ATS, passenger services, and predictive maintenance. A new line can receive a virtual service instance without a separate physical server for every application. Microservices can be expanded independently, and a multi-line cloud can share resources during different demand periods.

Train capacity is different. CBTC capacity is governed by safe separation, braking curves, train performance, dwell time, station conflicts, turnaround constraints, and operating rules. Cloud compute can support more complex optimization and larger network models, but it does not shorten a braking distance or reduce platform dwell time by itself.

The Alstom Urbalis product page reports up to 30% more capacity from reduced headways and up to 30% energy savings, but those are vendor-reported CBTC portfolio claims and are not cloud-specific. BART projects an increase from 24 to 30 trains per hour per direction as part of its conventional train-control modernization, again without attributing that result to cloud computing. ([Alstom Urbalis CBTC portfolio](https://www.alstom.com/solutions/signalling/urban-signalling/communications-based-train-control-world-leading-high-capacity-signalling); [BART capacity program](https://www.bart.gov/about/projects/traincontrol))

### Maintainability and lifecycle

The clearest cloud benefit is the possibility of separating software certification and lifecycle from a particular server model. Siemens presents DS3 as a platform whose certification can support hardware refresh on normal IT cycles, described in the supplied account as approximately five to seven years. This could reduce dependence on obsolete proprietary boards and improve spare-parts management.

However, railway certification makes change deliberate. A patch, operating-system update, hypervisor change, container image, configuration modification, or new monitoring agent may alter timing, interference, or behavior. A railway cybersecurity source notes that even a patch or configuration change to a SIL4 interlocking may require reassessment. ([Cylus railway safety and cybersecurity guidance](https://www.cylus.com/glossary/cenelec-en-50126-50128-50129))

Cloud operations therefore do not mean unrestricted continuous deployment. A railway needs version-controlled images, staged validation, configuration baselines, rollback, safety assessment, and clear responsibility between the signaling supplier, cloud operator, infrastructure manager, telecom provider, and maintenance organization.

### Cost: what the available proxies do and do not measure

There is no controlled, like-for-like dataset comparing the lifecycle cost of a complete cloud-hosted vital CBTC system with conventional on-premises CBTC. The available figures measure narrower proxies:

- Huawei reports traditional metro private wireless costs of more than CNY 1 million per kilometer in some deployments and proposes carrier-network leasing as a comparable business model.
- The Mumbai Metro Line 3 paper projects 40–50% lower capital expenditure for a 5G/FWA communications architecture than cable-intensive alternatives.
- Huawei’s Wuhan case reports halved station equipment-room construction costs, more than 10% labor-force reduction, and approximately 50% better IT-resource utilization.
- Siemens reports up to 20% higher operational efficiency and up to 30% energy savings in specified Signaling X and ATO contexts, without a published baseline or independent measurement.

These proxies demonstrate where savings might arise: less cable, fewer dedicated rooms, shared computing, fewer hardware types, and easier addition of services. They do not establish that cloud-vital CBTC will be cheaper after including data centers, redundant networks, private spectrum, cybersecurity, safety assessment, training, migration, software licenses, and long-term operations.

### Deployment flexibility and migration

Cloud architecture can make the logical system more flexible. A new line, additional train fleet, or new analytics function may be added through software and resource allocation. A backup center can assume services, and COTS hardware can be refreshed independently of the application.

The physical railway remains less flexible. A migration may require new antennas, onboard modems, wayside I/O, fiber, power, environmental protection, vehicle approvals, and night-time engineering possessions. The Mumbai project reports only three to four productive hours per night for underground work. A full route introduces repeated handovers, more trains, more edge nodes, and more failure combinations.

No supplied source quantifies workforce or training effects for cloud-hosted vital CBTC. The likely change is qualitative: railway maintainers and signaling engineers would need stronger skills in virtualization, network orchestration, identity management, observability, and incident response, while cloud and telecom personnel would need railway safety competence. Responsibility for a fault may also become more distributed. These implications are important, but a measured workforce comparison remains unavailable.

### Cybersecurity trade-off

Conventional systems are not automatically secure. Cisco warns that air-gapping does not prevent malware or unauthorized access, and legacy systems can contain vulnerabilities. Cloud architecture can improve asset visibility, logging, policy consistency, and security monitoring.

At the same time, cloud architecture adds management interfaces, shared infrastructure, software supply chains, virtualization layers, and remote-access paths. A private data center reduces public exposure but does not eliminate insider threats, misconfiguration, denial of service, supply-chain compromise, or common software vulnerabilities. The security architecture must therefore be designed with the safety architecture, not added after the cloud platform is selected.

## 7. Research maturity and near-term outlook

### Evidence maturity

The present landscape can be classified as follows.

| Evidence level | Named examples | What has been demonstrated | Remaining gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue or live service, non-cloud vital comparator | TSTCBTC 2.0 on Shanghai Metro Line 5; conventional CBTC programs such as BART | High-availability and brownfield CBTC operation | Does not demonstrate cloud-hosted vital control |
| Live SIL4 COTS signaling | Siemens DS3 at Achau | Safety-certified COTS interlocking in a mainline station | Urban cloud-CBTC scope and full train-control migration remain unshown |
| Live urban test-center demonstration | Siemens Signaling X at Singapore Rail Test Center | CBTC and interlocking operation on COTS/DS3 platform | No routine citywide revenue deployment or complete public acceptance |
| Live urban operational trial | Signaling X at Rostock | Cloud-native software-defined interlocking beneath a tram tunnel with paying passengers | Trial outcome, duration, coverage, acceptance, and full CBTC function set unavailable |
| Field-tested communications enabler | Mumbai Metro Line 3; CAF/Cellnex private 5G; HKIA 5G overlay; 5GRAIL/FRMCS | Throughput, latency, handover, slicing, or private-network integration in railway environments | No independent cloud-vital CBTC safety case |
| Operational cloud supervision or information systems | Wuhan, Shenzhen, and other urban-rail cloud platforms; cloud ATS architectures | Centralized data, information systems, monitoring, ATS, and O&M capabilities | Vital ATP, ATO, ZC, CI, and VOBC hosting not established |
| Research, simulation, or conceptual architecture | SDTC, ECCBTC, cloud-edge autonomous CBTC, AI and digital-twin studies | Models, simulations, reliability calculations, control algorithms, and proposed safety mechanisms | Field testing, certification, operational acceptance, and long-term reliability |

This classification resolves several apparent disagreements. Achau is a live SIL4 COTS interlocking reference, but it is not the same function or location as Rostock. Singapore is a test-center demonstration, while Rostock is a live urban trial. A private-5G CBTC validation demonstrates the bearer, not necessarily the cloud controller. A paper that proposes a SIL4 cloud architecture has not thereby established a certified SIL4 deployment.

### The most credible near-term direction

#### Private cloud with edge placement

The near-term architecture most consistent with the evidence is a private cloud-edge-end system. Non-vital applications and data platforms can use centralized cloud resources. ATS, integrated supervision, maintenance, and selected interlocking functions can be virtualized in controlled data centers. Time-sensitive or locally failure-critical functions can remain at the edge or on the train until communications and safety evidence justify further centralization.

This approach captures much of the practical value of cloud computing without making every train movement dependent on a distant central service.

#### Communications modernization

Private 5G, FRMCS, and more deterministic wireless networks are likely to expand before full cloud-CBTC. The Wuhan, Mumbai, CAF/Cellnex, Hitachi, HKIA, and 5GRAIL examples show substantial activity in private radio, slicing, mobility, and train-data integration.

The decisive metrics will be availability, handover interruption, packet-loss distribution, radio-jamming resilience, synchronization, and behavior under loaded cells. Peak throughput is less important for CBTC than bounded delay and predictable failure.

#### Virtualized signaling and COTS hardware

DS3 and Signaling X demonstrate the commercial direction of software-defined signaling. If the Rostock trial produces favorable results and independent acceptance evidence, it could encourage more urban operators to consider virtualized interlocking and cloud-ready signaling platforms. The likely first targets are interlocking, ATS, and other centralized or wayside functions rather than a complete cloud VOBC/ZC architecture.

#### Deterministic networking and safe clocks

5G and TSN integration, PTP, SyncE, 802.1AS, 802.1Qbv, frame replication, and railway protocols such as RaSTA and DDS will receive more attention. The industrial 5G-TSN experiments show that average latency is insufficient and that schedule-aware radio and core behavior are necessary. Railway use will require field testing in tunnels, stations, depots, and loaded multi-train conditions.

#### Digital twins for assurance and operations

Digital twins are likely to become important in safety assurance even if they do not directly control trains. They can provide:

- Virtual commissioning.
- Shadow-mode operation.
- Migration rehearsal.
- Fault and degraded-mode testing.
- Driverless-operation scenario generation.
- Maintenance and asset-health prediction.
- Operator and maintainer training.
- Post-incident reconstruction.

Their value is greatest when the twin is connected to real configuration and operational data, with clear separation between simulation recommendations and certified control commands.

#### AI as an advisory and optimization layer

AI will continue to expand in predictive maintenance, traffic management, passenger flow, incident response, and resource allocation. AI-assisted control may eventually influence train trajectories or virtually coupled trains, but the path to certified vital use will require constrained models, safety filters, deterministic fallbacks, explainability, data governance, adversarial testing, and evidence that the system remains safe when the AI is wrong.

The supplied evidence supports AI around CBTC more strongly than AI inside the safety authority itself.

### The evidence that would change the assessment

The conclusion that full urban cloud-CBTC remains unproven would change if a project published, independently assessed, and operationally accepted evidence covering:

1. The exact vital functions hosted in the cloud, including ATP, ATO, VOBC, ZC, CI, and interlocking scope.
2. A complete safety case and certification for the application, platform, network, interfaces, and operating environment.
3. End-to-end latency, jitter, packet loss, handover interruption, and time-synchronization distributions at relevant high percentiles.
4. Failover behavior for simultaneous server, network, wireless, time, power, and cyber failures.
5. Long-term availability and maintenance data from a full line or multi-line revenue operation.
6. Migration and coexistence results with legacy trains, wayside equipment, and radio systems.
7. Independent lifecycle-cost and workforce evidence.
8. Acceptance by the relevant transport authority and safety assessor.

As of 13 September 2026, the supplied evidence shows meaningful progress toward those conditions but does not show that all have been met in a routine urban deployment.

## Closing judgment

Cloud-based train control is best understood as a staged transformation of the CBTC technology stack. Cloud information systems, ATS, O&M, private 5G, edge computing, and virtualized infrastructure are already being deployed or field-tested. Siemens’ DS3 and Signaling X work shows that safety-related signaling can move toward COTS and private-cloud execution, while Rostock marks an important live urban trial.

The decisive boundary remains the difference between “cloud-connected CBTC” and “cloud-hosted vital CBTC.” The former is increasingly practical; the latter still requires independent evidence of deterministic communications, safe computation, failover, cybersecurity, migration, and certification. The near-term winning architecture is therefore likely to be private, redundant, edge-aware, and incrementally migrated, with cloud computing expanding first around the vital control core and only later assuming more of its functions as the safety case catches up.
